description:
FILÓMATAS LAB is an interdisciplinary team inspired by Renaissance thinking, bringing together science, technology, creativity, and education to democratize access to space education.

We aim to inspire scientific aspirations in children and young people from remote communities, proving that talent and curiosity know no boundaries and that anyone can dream of exploring the universe, no matter where their journey begins.

Small Beginnings. Infinite Possibilities.
summary:
Space education should not be a privilege reserved for well-equipped classrooms. Yet many children in rural and underserved communities remain excluded from the hands-on experiences that inspire scientific curiosity and future STEM careers.

NAUTI, developed by Filómatas LAB, responds to this challenge with an accessible, collaborative lunar mission simulator inspired by NASA scientific information.

Students become a mission team managing a simulated lunar base. Through narrative challenges, science-based trivia, and collective decisions, they balance water, energy, crew health, and scientific research. Their choices produce immediate and cumulative consequences, revealing how interconnected systems work and encouraging critical thinking, teamwork, and scientific reasoning.

Beyond software, NAUTI proposes reusing functional smartphones with simple handmade cardboard supports, making immersive STEM learning possible without expensive equipment.

NAUTI is more than a space simulation. It is a scalable educational concept designed to turn technological limitations into opportunities for scientific exploration, empowering underserved communities to participate in the future of space education.
details:
We created NAUTI because we believe every child deserves access to STEAM education, no matter where they live. In Paraguay, many rural schools have limited resources for hands-on science activities. We wanted to create something affordable, fun, and useful for these students, with the possibility of reaching schools across Latin America.

What does NAUTI do? NAUTI is a web-based Moon mission simulator where students work together to manage a lunar base. They face challenges, discuss solutions, and make decisions as a team. The mission includes four connected indicators: water, energy, crew health, and scientific research. Their choices change these resources, and some decisions affect future events. Students learn that every choice matters.

How do students learn? NAUTI combines an interactive story, scientific questions, and teamwork. Students follow a mission guided by NAUTI, our friendly space character. We included scientific information from NASA, with references and direct links to original NASA sources. For example, students can explore NASA's research on recovering 98% of water aboard the International Space Station. They can also consult information cards about water, energy, and health. This helps students use real scientific evidence, discuss possible solutions, and understand how their decisions affect the mission.

How did we build it? We used Design Thinking to understand the educational problem, develop ideas, and improve our prototype. Our team tested the experience internally and made changes to the instructions, mission length, resource indicators, and game mechanics. We wanted students to see both immediate and long-term consequences, without making the activity too long or difficult for classroom use.

What tools did we use? We developed NAUTI using Google AI Studio and Super Intelligence (SI) tools. ChatGPT helped us plan the learning experience, create educational content, and solve technical problems. We also used GitHub to organize our code and explored collaboration with Codex. Our web project includes HTML and other application components. Google development credits provided through the NASA Space Apps Challenge supported our work. We also used official NASA scientific resources to build educational content based on real space research.

What makes NAUTI different? NAUTI is designed for teamwork rather than individual competition. The app is already available in English, Spanish, and Guaraní, allowing students to choose their language. Including Guaraní is especially important to us because NAUTI was created in Paraguay, where language is part of our cultural identity. We also explored using old smartphones and handmade cardboard stands to create low-cost mission stations, making STEAM learning more accessible.

What did we consider? We focused on accessibility, cost, language, teamwork, scientific accuracy, and student engagement. We designed the interface for smartphones in landscape mode, with clear resource indicators and a friendly visual style. We also wanted the story to be interesting enough to keep students engaged while giving them time to think, discuss, and learn together.

What comes next? We want to test NAUTI with teachers and students in Paraguay, improve it with their feedback, and create more missions and classroom materials. Our dream is to bring this experience to schools across Latin America, especially those with fewer opportunities to explore STEAM. We hope NAUTI can inspire children to see science as something they can be part of, regardless of where they come from. Because curiosity has no boundaries.
